mercury_by_fish.detail: Methylmercury accumulates up the food chain, so a fish that ate thousands of smaller fish across twenty years carries far more than one that lived two years on plankton. Ocean fish also carry selenium, which counteracts mercury, and studies that count mercury alone leave it out. Small wild fish such as sardines, anchovies, herring and mackerel give the most for the least. Anything about a personal medical situation belongs with a doctor. Canned light tuna is usually skipjack.
mercury_by_fish.science: Mercury accumulates up the food chain, tracking size and lifespan. Albacore, yellowfin and halibut sit in the middle. Ocean fish also carry selenium, which counteracts mercury. Low mercury is not the whole picture: shrimp and tilapia are low in omega-3s, wild salmon and sardines high. Anything medical is a doctor’s call.
buying_tips: Mercury builds with size and lifespan, so big long-lived predators carry the most.
Lowest: sardines, anchovies, salmon, shrimp, scallops, tilapia, cod, pollock, catfish, canned light tuna.
Middle: albacore and yellowfin tuna, halibut, grouper, snapper, mahi mahi.
Highest: swordfish, shark, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, bigeye tuna, Gulf tilefish.
‘Light’ tuna is usually skipjack, lower in mercury than ‘white’ albacore.
Pregnant, nursing or feeding a young child? Anything medical is a doctor’s call.
Sardines and canned salmon, bones left in, are shelf-stable and low on the chain. Canned is the cheapest way to eat either one.
watch_out: Low mercury is not the whole picture. Shrimp, catfish, tilapia, clams and scallops are low in mercury and also low in omega-3s. Wild salmon, sardines, mussels and mackerel are low in mercury and high in omega-3s.
The real exceptions are the giants: swordfish, marlin and other big billfish that live for decades.

seafood_certifications.why: Each seal answers one narrow question about stock or farm practice. None speaks to freshness or the fish as food.

seafood_certifications.detail: Each seal answers one question. MSC audits whether a wild fishery is managed so the stock holds. ASC and BAP audit farms, and BAP’s stars count the audited links from plant up to feed mill. None tells anything about the fish in front of you: how fresh it is, what it ate, or how it was handled. A farmed salmon can carry a farm seal and still sit on traditional avoid lists. The origin, wild or farmed, and how it was caught say more than a seal.
seafood_certifications.kristy_take: A seal is a stock or farm audit, not a health claim. The origin and the catch method say more.
seafood_certifications.science: MSC audits wild fisheries for stock management and habitat impact. ASC and BAP audit farms; both set a floor. BAP’s stars run from plant up to farm, hatchery and feed mill. No seal is a health claim.

venison_game.decision: Venison from a refrigerated processor, cooked with a pastured fat.
venison_game.why: Venison is lean, and traditional guides say eat meat with its fat. Cold handling at the processor decides how it keeps.
venison_game.kristy_take: Plan a meal within two or three days of bringing unfrozen venison home. Cook it with butter, lard or tallow, whole cuts to 145°F, ground game to 160°F.
pick_steps: Pass on meat that is bruised, discolored, or has hair, dirt or bone fragments.
Keep the fat on, and use unfrozen venison within two or three days.
buying_tips: Game often comes through small shops, where cold handling decides its safety.
Ask whether the processor handles each animal individually.
Choose a processor with fully refrigerated facilities.
Use unfrozen venison within two or three days.
Venison is lean; pair it with butter, lard or tallow from pastured animals.

white_fish.detail: Seafood must be labeled with an acceptable market name for its species, so the name is the check. Wild cod or halibut by name, fresh or frozen at sea, is the pick. Tilapia, catfish and trout from farms sit on traditional avoid lists. Fillets should sit on ice, not buried in it. For frozen packs, skip tears, ice crystals, liquid inside, or soft flesh.
white_fish.science: Seafood must be labeled with an acceptable market name for its species. Color alone does not show freshness, because diet, environment and color fixatives all change it.
white_fish.tier_note: The species name and firm flesh decide a white fish fillet, not its color.
buying_tips: A fillet is hard to identify by eye, so the species name does that work.
Look for how it was caught and the species, on the sign or label.
Ask the counter which species the fillet is.
Press the flesh and check that it springs back.
Skip fillets with dried, dark or discolored edges.
Dry packed fillets: see Scallops.
Wild cod or halibut by name, fresh or frozen at sea, is the pick.

crab.detail: Crabs spoil rapidly after death, so only live crabs should be chosen. Keep live crabs in a ventilated container, never an airtight bag, and use them within 1 to 2 days. Crab is among the richest sources of vitamins, with selenium, zinc and B12. The yellow ‘butter’ inside holds the fat-soluble part. Soft-shell crabs are blue crabs that just molted. Imitation crab is surimi, made from cooked Alaska pollock.
crab.science: Crabs spoil rapidly after death, so only live crabs should be chosen. A crab that does not move may have died. Cooked crab shows its quality in shell color and smell. Imitation crab is surimi, made from cooked Alaska pollock, not crab meat.
crab.tier_note: Leg movement on live crab and shell color on cooked crab are the buying checks.
buying_tips: Crabs spoil fast after death, and moving legs show the crab is alive.
Check that live crabs move their legs.
Look for bright orange to red shells on cooked crab.
Smell cooked crab and skip any with an off odor.
Buy unpackaged cooked crab only from a case kept apart from raw seafood.
Ask for whole crab, or cracked and cleaned, and keep the yellow butter.
sources: Weston A. Price Foundation: Crab, a high-vitamin food (Ramiel Nagel)

lobster.detail: Only live lobsters should be chosen, since they spoil rapidly after death. Raw lobster flesh should be clear and pearl-like, with little or no odor. Hard-shell and soft-shell lobsters are the same animal at different growth stages. A soft-shell lobster recently shed its old shell, so water sits between shell and meat. Use live lobster within 1 to 2 days.
lobster.tier_note: The movement and tail checks show a lobster is alive and fresh.
buying_tips: A dead lobster spoils fast, and a tail that curls under shows a lively one.
Ask the counter to lift the lobster and watch the tail.
Check that the claws and legs move.
Pick frozen tails that are hard-frozen, with clear white meat.
Skip frozen packs that are torn or show ice crystals.
The green tomalley holds the fat-soluble vitamins; eat it when the water is clean.

buying_tips: Wet scallops are treated with phosphate and water so they hold extra water.
Read the ingredients for a phosphate and water.
Ask the counter whether the scallops are dry.
Skip packs sitting in excess liquid.
Smell for a sweetish odor.
Dayboat scallops, under 24 hours at sea with no ice touching them, are the top rung.
watch_out: Wet scallops hold extra water.
Loose scallops at the counter may carry no ingredient list, so ask.
‘Dry’ is not policed on its own, and ‘diver’ is mostly mislabeled drag catch. Ask the boat or the port.

buying_tips: The tag names the certified shipper, the harvest date and the harvest area.

Tap any open shell and check that it closes.
Skip cracked or broken shells.

seafood_counter.why: The species name is what a seafood label must get right, and it is the first thing to ask.
seafood_counter.detail: Buy fish refrigerated or on a thick bed of fresh ice, preferably under a cover. Fish should smell fresh and mild, not fishy, sour or ammonia-like. Unpackaged cooked seafood belongs in its own case or behind dividers from raw. Ask the species, wild or farmed, the country, and when it landed.
seafood_counter.science: A seafood label must get the species name right. Unpackaged cooked seafood belongs in its own case or behind dividers from raw. Ask the species, wild or farmed, the country, and when it landed.
seafood_counter.tier_note: Smell, ice, gills and a named species are the counter checks.
buying_tips: Red gills mean recently slaughtered; brown, gray or green means past fresh.
Ask the counter for the species name.
Ask the counter where it came from and whether it was farmed.
Check that the fish sits on ice or in a refrigerated case.
Check that cooked seafood is kept apart from raw.
Ask the counter ‘was this previously frozen?’ The answer is often yes.
Buy frozen and thaw at home on your own schedule.
Don’t re-freeze fish that was sold thawed.
Smell it. Clean and briny is right. Sharp, fishy or ammonia is not.
Whole fish: clear domed eyes, bright red gills, tight scales, flesh that springs back.
Fillets: a translucent sheen, flakes holding together, no browning at the edge.
It should sit on plenty of ice, not in a pool of its own liquid.
Ask the counter when it came in and whether it was previously frozen. Both are fair questions.
At the counter, ask for dry packed scallops and fillets; ‘wet’ means soaked in sodium tripolyphosphate, which adds water weight.
Tuna labeled ‘tasteless smoke’ or ‘treated with carbon monoxide’ stays red as it ages; untreated tuna browns.
Ask the counter the species, wild or farmed, the country, and when it landed.

labels_decoded.meaning: The acceptable market name for the fish; ask for it when the sign is vague.
Frozen then thawed for display; common and fine, just don’t re-freeze.
Never frozen, but possibly several days old depending on transit.
Flakes separating on a fillet. A sign it has aged.
